prompt: What does a layer 4 balancer read before it chooses a server?
hint: It never looks inside the stream.

choices.text: The request's path and its Host header
choices.why: Reading the request is what a layer 7 proxy does.

choices.text: Addresses and ports
choices.why: Right. The connection is all it has to go on.

choices.text: The load on each server's processor
choices.why: Nothing in a packet says how busy a server is.

choices.text: The client's cookies
choices.why: Cookies are inside the HTTP request, which a layer 4 balancer does not read.

prompt: Why can a layer 4 balancer carry HTTPS without holding the site's certificate?
hint: What would it need the certificate for?

choices.text: Balancing HTTPS needs no certificate at any layer
choices.why: A layer 7 balancer that reads HTTPS has to hold it and decrypt.

choices.text: It decrypts with the server's public key
choices.why: A public key decrypts nothing of the session; and it decrypts nothing at all.

choices.text: It never reads inside the TCP stream
choices.why: Right. It forwards encrypted bytes it has no reason to understand.

choices.text: Port 443 is excluded from inspection by the standard
choices.why: No standard exempts a port; it simply does not look.

prompt: One site must send requests for /api/ to one group of servers and everything else to another, over HTTPS. What does the balancer need?

choices.text: Layer 7, with the certificate, to read the path
choices.why: Right. The path is inside the encrypted request, so it has to be decrypted to be read.

choices.text: Layer 4 with a rule for port 443
choices.why: Both groups are on port 443; the port cannot tell them apart.

choices.text: A source hash on the client's address
choices.why: The same client asks for /api/ and for pages; its address says nothing about which.

choices.text: Least connections across the two groups
choices.why: That chooses by load, not by what was asked for.

prompt: Six requests under round robin went to web1, web2, web3, web1, web2, web3. What decided that order?

choices.text: Which server had answered fastest
choices.why: Round robin measures nothing about the servers.

choices.text: The order the servers are listed in
choices.why: Right. It takes the next name in the list, and starts again after the last.

choices.text: Each server's open connections
choices.why: That is least connections.

choices.text: A hash of the laptop's address
choices.why: A hash would have sent all six to one server.

prompt: A round-robin backend has three servers with weights 3, 1 and 1. Out of 100 requests, how many go to the server with weight 3?
When is plain round robin a poor fit?

choices.text: When the servers are identical machines
choices.why: That is exactly its case: equal servers, equal shares.

choices.text: When there are more than two servers
choices.why: The number of servers changes nothing; it just takes longer to go round.

choices.text: When some requests cost far more than others
choices.why: Right. It counts requests, not work, so a busy server keeps getting its turn.

choices.text: When the clients are behind NAT
choices.why: NAT hurts a source hash; round robin never looks at the client's address.

prompt: With balance leastconn, web1 received none of the four ordinary requests. Why?

choices.text: It was still sending slow.txt
choices.why: Right. One open connection against none on the other two.

choices.text: web1 had stopped answering
choices.why: It was answering; it was busy with the download.

choices.text: web1's weight was lower than the others'
choices.why: The leastconn backend sets no weights at all.

choices.text: Least connections skips the first server in the list
choices.why: The list order does not matter to it; the counts do.

prompt: `show stat`, cut to three fields, printed `web,web2,1`. What is the 1?

choices.text: Requests web2 has served since HAProxy started
choices.why: That total is another field; this one is a count of now.

choices.text: web2's weight in the backend
choices.why: The backend sets no weights, and the others print 0.

choices.text: Health checks web2 has failed
choices.why: This backend has no checks at all.

choices.text: Connections open to web2 at that moment
choices.why: Right. The slow download, which is why the next request goes elsewhere.

prompt: A site serves only small pages, and every connection closes within a millisecond. What changes if it moves from round robin to least connections?
hint: What are the counts between requests?

choices.text: The fastest server starts getting most of the traffic
choices.why: It counts connections, not speed, and with every count at zero there is nothing to prefer.

choices.text: Almost nothing, since the counts sit at zero
choices.why: Right. Least connections only differs when some connections outlast others.

choices.text: Every request goes to the first server, since all are tied
choices.why: Ties are shared out in turn, which is round robin again.

choices.text: It slows down, because counting costs time
choices.why: Keeping a counter per server is negligible next to a request.

prompt: Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest ___ connections at that moment.
Under balance source, four of the five clients landed on web1 and none on web3. Why?
hint: Think of a coin thrown five times.

choices.text: web1 had the highest weight
choices.why: That backend sets no weights.

choices.text: The hash favours lower addresses
choices.why: A hash has no favourites; that is the point of it.

choices.text: Five addresses are too few for a hash to spread evenly
choices.why: Right. Evenness appears over many addresses, not five.

choices.text: web3 was down during the test
choices.why: Nothing was stopped in that run; web3 answered in the next one.

prompt: Two hundred people at head office use a site behind a source-hash balancer. How are they spread over its servers?
hint: Which address does the balancer see?

choices.text: Evenly, since two hundred is plenty of clients
choices.why: Two hundred people, but one address after NAT.

choices.text: All on one server, since they share 203.0.113.2
choices.why: Right. The whole office is one client to the hash.

choices.text: By their own addresses, 192.168.10.x
choices.why: Those never reach the balancer; hq's NAT rewrites them.

choices.text: At random, a new server for each request
choices.why: A hash is the opposite of random: the same input, the same server.

prompt: A fourth server is added to a `balance source` backend. What happens to the clients already using it?
hint: The hash is divided by the total weight.

choices.text: Most of them move to a different server
choices.why: Right. A new divisor gives most addresses a new remainder. hash-type consistent limits that.

choices.text: None move; only new clients reach the fourth
choices.why: The balancer keeps no memory of who went where; it recomputes every time.

choices.text: They all move to the new server
choices.why: The new server gets its share, a quarter, not everybody.

choices.text: Only web1's clients move
choices.why: The remainder changes for addresses on every server.

prompt: Match each client to the address lb1 hashes for it.
hint: Each office and home has one public address.

prompt: What did HAProxy add to its first reply to a client with no cookie?

choices.text: The chosen server's IP address, in a header
choices.why: The cookie's value is a label, w1, and tells nothing about the network.

choices.text: A cookie saying SERVERID=w1
choices.why: Right. The label of the server round robin had just picked.

choices.text: A login session id from the application
choices.why: The application knows nothing about it; insert means HAProxy writes it.

choices.text: Nothing until the client asked for a cookie
choices.why: A client never asks; the balancer sets it on the first reply.

prompt: After web3's nginx stopped, the client with SERVERID=w3 got a 503 while web1 and web2 were running. Why?

choices.text: web1 and web2 were full
choices.why: They were idle; the request was never offered to them.

choices.text: The cookie had expired
choices.why: It was sent by hand with -b and was obeyed exactly.

choices.text: No health check had told HAProxy web3 was gone
choices.why: Right. It sent the request where the cookie said and had nowhere else it was allowed to go.

choices.text: A 503 is what redispatch returns
choices.why: Redispatch was not configured yet; once it was, the client got web1.

prompt: With checks and redispatch, the pinned client was moved to web1. What became of the basket the application kept in web3's memory?

choices.text: HAProxy copied it across to web1
choices.why: A balancer moves requests, never a server's memory.

choices.text: It travels inside the SERVERID cookie
choices.why: The cookie holds two characters, w1, and nothing else.

choices.text: It comes back once web3 is started again
choices.why: A restarted process starts with empty memory, and the client now carries w1 anyway.

choices.text: It was lost with web3
choices.why: Right. That is why state belongs in a store every server shares.

prompt: Which lines of the fixed backend were needed to move the pinned client instead of failing it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: option redispatch
choices.why: Right: it allows another server when the named one is down.

choices.text: balance roundrobin
choices.why: It was there before the 503 as well.

choices.text: check inter 1s, on each server
choices.why: Right: without checks HAProxy cannot know web3 is down.

choices.text: cookie SERVERID insert indirect nocache
choices.why: That line is what pins the client; it was there before the 503 too.

prompt: With checks and redispatch in place, put in order what happens when the pinned server dies.
hint: The balancer has to find out first.
items: A health check fails and web3 is marked down
trap: The check has to fail before the request comes, or the request meets the dead server as the 503 did.

prompt: Match each balance setting to what it decides by.
hint: Three rules, three pieces of information.

pairs.right: The next name in the list
A hash of the client's address

prompt: A video service streams sessions of very different lengths from three equal servers, to viewers all over the internet. Which balance setting fits best?

choices.text: roundrobin, since the servers are equal
choices.why: Equal servers, unequal work: turns would pile long streams on whoever draws them.

choices.text: leastconn
choices.why: Right. It sends each new session to the server with the fewest still running.

choices.text: source, to keep each viewer on one server
choices.why: Viewers behind carrier NAT share addresses, and whole groups would land together.

choices.text: roundrobin with weight 2 on the first server
choices.why: The servers are equal, so a weight would only unbalance them.
